title: The readings and the psalm
hookLine: Sundays run a three-year cycle so most of the Bible is read aloud
last: GLORY TO GOD IN THE HIGHEST.

cards: The Gloria ends, the priest says a short opening prayer, and everyone sits down. That's the signal. The first part of the Mass, the gathering, the mercy and the praise, is over.
Now comes the second: listening. A person walks up to a stand called the ambo. Very often it isn't the priest.
It's a parishioner, a teacher or a retired mailman or a nervous sixteen-year-old, reading from a big book to a room full of people. And the passage wasn't chosen by the priest that week, or by them.
It was chosen decades ago, for this exact Sunday, by a plan that runs across three years.

teach.b: Lectionary comes from the Latin lectio, a reading. It's the book of readings for Mass, laid out day by day.
At the Second Vatican Council in the 1960s, the bishops asked for the treasures of the Bible to be opened up much more richly to the people. So a new lectionary was built, in use from 1970.
On a Sunday there are four readings, counting the psalm. First, usually from the Old Testament, chosen to echo the day's Gospel.
Then a psalm, sung or said: a cantor sings the verses, and everyone answers with a short refrain. Then a reading from one of the apostles' letters, often Paul. Then the Gospel.
The Sundays run in a three-year cycle. Year A reads mostly from Matthew. Year B, Mark.
Year C, Luke. John comes in around the great seasons, Lent and Easter, and fills out the short year of Mark.
So over three years, a Catholic who comes every week hears the Gospels in turn and a wide sweep of the rest of the Bible.
Not every word, but far more than before the reform, when one year of readings repeated over and over. Weekdays have their own cycle.

And on any given Sunday, Roman Rite parishes around the world, in many languages, are reading the same passages. At the end of each reading, the reader says, in the old Latin, Verbum Domini, the word of the Lord.
And the people answer, Deo gratias, thanks be to God.

how: At Sunday Mass, lay readers usually proclaim the first and second readings from the ambo, a cantor leads the responsorial psalm, and the readings follow a three-year cycle (Years A, B and C) shared by Roman Rite parishes worldwide.

o: the letters of Paul are read instead.

practice: Here's a line from the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths." Say it again in your head, slower, and notice which word catches: lamp, feet, paths.
You don't have to decide what it means, just carry it for a minute; if you pray, you can let it become your prayer.
